name: Safari Chic

influenced_by: real 19th-20th century European expedition and colonial-administrator dress

eras: roots in 19th-20th c. expedition dress; recurring fashion revival

media.title: Yves Saint Laurent's 1968 safari jacket collection
media.note: the fashion-history moment most credited with bringing safari style into mainstream haute couture

reacts_against: nothing contemporaneous; safari chic repeatedly borrows real garments from a specific colonial-era context and recasts them as adventure glamour, a move that later fashion criticism has scrutinized for what it leaves out of that history.
article: Safari chic takes its garments directly from real 19th-20th century European expedition and colonial-administrator dress — khaki drill cloth (chosen originally for its dust-concealing color), pith helmets, utility pockets — clothing designed for a specific historical context of European exploration and colonial administration in Africa and South Asia. Yves Saint Laurent's 1968 safari jacket collection is the fashion-history moment most credited with lifting that wardrobe into mainstream high fashion, stripped of its original administrative function and recast as glamorous adventure-wear for a wealthy European clientele. The style has resurfaced on runways periodically since, and fashion criticism in more recent decades has increasingly scrutinized that recurring move — borrowing colonial-era military and administrative dress for pure aesthetic glamour tends to leave out the historical context those garments actually came from, a tension safari chic shares with military chic more broadly.

findings: mostly muted — about 68% of the measured color is low-saturation (greys, dusty tones)
measured.caveat: Colors measured from Aesthetics Wiki images as photographed and displayed on screen; actual materials vary, and screen colors are approximate.
